checklist.title: Write a one-page plan and a first-year budget
checklist.text: List what you will sell, to whom, and every cost before and after opening day. Plan cash for at least three months of fixed costs after you open. NYC Small Business Services offers free courses, lease review and one-on-one help.
checklist.agency: NYC Department of Small Business Services

checklist.title: Scout storefronts: look for a former cafe
checklist.text: About 800 sq ft holds 18-24 seats. A former cafe keeps its plumbing, ventilation and bathroom: a light renovation runs near $90 per sq ft instead of $200-$300. Typical asking rents for 800 sq ft: about $3,000 a month in outer Queens, $6,000 on a Brooklyn side street, $22,000 in prime Manhattan.

checklist.title: Check the Certificate of Occupancy before you sign
checklist.text: The building's Certificate of Occupancy must allow an eating and drinking place; buildings from before 1938 may need a Letter of No Objection instead. Also check electrical capacity, the grease interceptor, an accessible restroom and whether the block is landmarked. Make the lease depend on getting your permits.

checklist.title: Choose a legal form
checklist.text: An LLC keeps business debts apart from your home and savings; a sole proprietorship costs nothing to form but leaves you personally liable. Most small shops in New York start as a single-member LLC taxed on the owner's personal return.

checklist.title: Form the LLC: file Articles of Organization
checklist.text: File online for $200; the filing receipt usually arrives the same day. Adopt an operating agreement within 90 days. If the shop name differs from the LLC name, also file an assumed name certificate ($25).
checklist.agency: NYS Department of State, Division of Corporations

checklist.title: Publish the LLC notice
checklist.text: Within 120 days, publish a notice in two newspapers for six weeks, then file a Certificate of Publication ($50). All-in packages cost about $1,795 in Manhattan, $1,475 in Brooklyn and $1,195 in Queens. Skip it and the LLC's authority to do business is suspended.

checklist.title: Get an EIN
checklist.text: Apply on IRS.gov: free, issued in minutes. You need it for the bank, payroll and the sales tax registration. Never pay a website for an EIN.

checklist.title: Open a business bank account
checklist.text: Bring the EIN letter, the LLC filing receipt and the operating agreement. Run every business dollar through this account, and open a second one only for the sales tax you collect.

checklist.title: Register for sales tax: Certificate of Authority
checklist.text: Apply online at least 20 days before your first taxable sale; there is no fee. Selling without the certificate can cost up to $500 for the first day and $200 for each day after, up to $10,000. Display it in the shop.
checklist.agency: NYS Department of Taxation and Finance

checklist.title: Negotiate and sign the lease
checklist.text: Before you sign, check the permitted use, who pays property tax increases and repairs, free rent during build-out, the right to assign the lease, and the personal guaranty. A deposit of two months is common; new businesses are often asked for three or more.
checklist.agency: NYC Department of Small Business Services (free lease review)

checklist.title: Design and build out
checklist.text: An architect files plans, licensed plumbers and electricians pull the permits. Budget $70,000 for a light renovation of a former cafe plus about 10% for drawings and filings. Expect 6-14 weeks for permits and 8-24 weeks of construction, with rent due once any free-rent period ends.

checklist.title: Buy the required insurance
checklist.text: Workers' compensation and disability coverage are mandatory once you have one employee, and permit applications ask for proof. Landlords also require general liability; a business owner's policy for a small shop averages about $126 a month nationally.

checklist.title: Pass the Food Protection Course
checklist.text: Take the free 15-lesson online course and pay $24 for the in-person exam. A certified supervisor must be in the shop every hour it is open, so certify yourself and at least one more person. You need the certificate or a course registration to apply for the permit.

checklist.title: Get your Food Service Establishment Permit
checklist.text: Apply online with proof of workers' compensation and disability insurance, the sales tax Certificate of Authority and the Food Protection Certificate. The fee is $280 a year. You may open on the 22nd day after applying; call for a pre-operational inspection if you want to open sooner.
checklist.agency: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH)

checklist.title: Grease interceptor and private carter
checklist.text: Have a licensed plumber confirm the grease interceptor is the right size. Sign a contract with one of the three private carters authorized for your commercial waste zone and post the decal: the city does not pick up business trash.
checklist.agency: NYC Department of Environmental Protection; NYC Department of Sanitation

checklist.title: Check the sign rules before you order a sign
checklist.text: A wall sign of 6 sq ft or less needs no sign permit. A bigger or illuminated sign must be filed with the Department of Buildings and hung by a licensed sign hanger, and the landlord usually has to approve it.

checklist.title: Optional: apply for sidewalk seating
checklist.text: Sidewalk tables need a Dining Out NYC license: $1,050 for four years plus a $1,500 refundable deposit and a yearly fee per square foot. Apply early, but plan year one without outdoor seats: more than half of approved restaurants waited over 19 months.
checklist.agency: NYC Department of Transportation (Dining Out NYC)

checklist.title: Set up bookkeeping and a tax calendar
checklist.text: Pick accounting software or a bookkeeper before the first sale. Put the dates in a calendar: payroll tax deposits every month, sales tax and unemployment returns every quarter, estimated income tax four times a year, the $25 LLC fee once a year.
checklist.agency: IRS; NYS Department of Taxation and Finance

checklist.title: Buy equipment and furniture
checklist.text: A new basic set costs about $36,500 before tax and delivery: espresso machine $7,600, two grinders $4,200, fridges and pastry case $3,800, sinks, ice machine, dishwasher, register, 20 chairs and 10 tables. Order the machine first: delivery takes 2-4 weeks. Used gear from a closing cafe cuts the bill.

checklist.title: Line up suppliers and the opening order
checklist.text: Pick a wholesale roaster (many train your staff and service the machine), a dairy distributor, a wholesale bakery that delivers before 7am, and a source for cups and lids. Open accounts two to three weeks ahead; the first order runs $3,000-$5,000.

checklist.title: Set up the register and card payments
checklist.text: A Square register costs about $900; processing is 2.5%-2.6% plus 15 cents per tap. Program each menu item as taxable or not, switch on tip reporting, and connect payroll so tips and hours flow into pay stubs.

checklist.title: Hire legally: Form I-9, pay notice, payroll
checklist.text: For every hire: complete Form I-9 with original identity documents, give a written notice of the pay rate and payday, withhold taxes and hand over a pay stub every payday. Register with New York State as an employer for unemployment insurance.

checklist.title: Hire and train baristas
checklist.text: Four baristas cover a 12-hour day at 200 orders. Minimum wage is $17.00; the model pays $21 plus tips. Pay for training and trial shifts, give each hire a written pay notice, and schedule to avoid overtime and days longer than 10 hours.

checklist.title: Open your doors
checklist.text: Open once the permit is in hand or on the 22nd day after applying. Post the permit, keep the Food Protection Certificate and the pest control contract in the shop, and expect an unannounced first inspection. Keep three months of fixed costs in the bank: the first months are slower than the plan.

suppliers.what: Wholesale roasted beans, usually with barista training and equipment service included
suppliers.whereToFind: Ask the cafes you like who roasts for them, then visit two or three roasters for a cupping. Most have a wholesale page and deliver weekly across the city.
suppliers.examples: Partners Coffee, Joe Coffee Company, Brooklyn Roasting Company, Variety Coffee Roasters, Devocion, Counter Culture Coffee
suppliers.note: Seen on the Partners Coffee wholesale page: barista education, in-house service technicians, equipment and delivery across New York City. Names are well-known examples from general knowledge of the New York market, not endorsements and not checked in this session unless a link is given; compare at least three quotes.

suppliers.what: Whole milk, half-and-half, oat and almond milk delivered several times a week
suppliers.whereToFind: Foodservice distributors that already deliver on your street; your roaster and neighboring cafes know which trucks pass by. Small volumes: a cash-and-carry warehouse.
suppliers.examples: Baldor Specialty Foods, Dairyland (The Chefs' Warehouse), Battenkill Valley Creamery, Restaurant Depot for oat milk by the case
suppliers.note: Seen on Baldor's site: a specialty food distributor carrying dairy, bakery, produce and kitchen supplies for business customers. Names are well-known examples from general knowledge of the New York market, not endorsements and not checked in this session unless a link is given; compare at least three quotes.

suppliers.what: Croissants, muffins, cookies and sandwiches baked by a licensed wholesale bakery and delivered before opening
suppliers.whereToFind: Wholesale programs of local bakeries: ask for a sample box and the minimum order. Buying from a licensed source keeps you inside the Health Code; home baking does not.
suppliers.examples: Balthazar Bakery, Bien Cuit, Ceci-Cela, Colson Patisserie, Pain d'Avignon, Orwashers, Amy's Bread
suppliers.note: The rule behind it was seen in the penalty schedule: food from an unapproved source or home cooked is a public health hazard ($400-$600). Names are well-known examples from general knowledge of the New York market, not endorsements and not checked in this session unless a link is given; compare at least three quotes.

suppliers.what: Espresso machine, grinders, refrigeration, sinks, dishwasher, shelving
suppliers.whereToFind: Online restaurant supply stores for list prices; the restaurant supply shops on the Bowery in Manhattan to see things in person; your roaster for the espresso machine, often with a service contract.
suppliers.examples: WebstaurantStore, KaTom, Visions Espresso, Restaurant Depot, Bowery restaurant supply shops
suppliers.note: Prices in this pack were seen at WebstaurantStore and Visions Espresso on November 14, 2026. Names are well-known examples from general knowledge of the New York market, not endorsements and not checked in this session unless a link is given; compare at least three quotes.

suppliers.what: Second-hand machines, fridges and furniture at roughly half the new price
suppliers.whereToFind: Cafes that are closing (ask brokers and landlords), restaurant equipment auctions, used dealers on the Bowery, Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist. Have a technician test an espresso machine before you pay.
suppliers.examples: Restaurant auction houses, used equipment dealers on the Bowery, the previous tenant of your space
suppliers.note: The "half price" figure is my rough estimate. The research notes' cheapest opening budget assumes part of the previous cafe's equipment is kept. Names are well-known examples from general knowledge of the New York market, not endorsements and not checked in this session unless a link is given; compare at least three quotes.

suppliers.what: Cups, lids, sleeves, napkins, bags, cleaning chemicals, gloves
suppliers.whereToFind: Order online by the case, or load a van at a cash-and-carry warehouse in Brooklyn, Queens or the Bronx. Membership is free for businesses.
suppliers.note: Seen: Restaurant Depot is a wholesale cash-and-carry supplier with free membership; 12 oz hot cups cost $45.99 per 1,000 at WebstaurantStore. Names are well-known examples from general knowledge of the New York market, not endorsements and not checked in this session unless a link is given; compare at least three quotes.

suppliers.what: Point-of-sale system, card reader, online ordering, tip and sales tax reports
suppliers.whereToFind: Compare the monthly plan and the per-tap fee on the providers' own pricing pages; on small tickets the fixed cents matter more than the percentage.
suppliers.note: Seen in Square's fee table: 2.6% + 15 cents (Free), 2.5% + 15 cents (Plus), 2.4% + 15 cents (Premium) per in-person payment. Names are well-known examples from general knowledge of the New York market, not endorsements and not checked in this session unless a link is given; compare at least three quotes.

suppliers.what: Business owner's policy, workers' compensation, disability and paid family leave coverage
suppliers.whereToFind: An independent broker who insures restaurants can quote several carriers at once. The New York State Insurance Fund writes workers' compensation and disability policies for any employer.
suppliers.examples: A local independent broker, Insureon, New York State Insurance Fund (NYSIF)
suppliers.note: Seen at Insureon: coffee shops pay on average $126 a month for a business owner's policy and $88 for workers' compensation across the US. Names are well-known examples from general knowledge of the New York market, not endorsements and not checked in this session unless a link is given; compare at least three quotes.

suppliers.what: Bookkeeper or accountant who knows restaurants; free city help with leases, permits and plans
suppliers.whereToFind: Ask other owners on your block for their accountant. NYC Small Business Services gives free lease review, legal advice, business courses and a team that walks restaurants through permits.
suppliers.examples: NYC Small Business Services and its NYC Business Express Service Team, a local accountant with restaurant clients
suppliers.note: Seen on the NYC Business restaurant page: free commercial lease assistance, free legal advice, free business courses and the NYC Business Express Service Team. Names are well-known examples from general knowledge of the New York market, not endorsements and not checked in this session unless a link is given; compare at least three quotes.

suppliers.what: Monthly service by a state-licensed exterminator, with a written contract kept in the shop
suppliers.whereToFind: Ask neighboring restaurants; check that the company is licensed by the state. Expect $100-$300 a month for a small cafe.
suppliers.note: Seen at a local exterminator's 2026 price guide: $100-$300 a month for a small NYC cafe, $250-$600 for a first treatment. Names are well-known examples from general knowledge of the New York market, not endorsements and not checked in this session unless a link is given; compare at least three quotes.

suppliers.what: Private carter for trash, recycling and food scraps
suppliers.whereToFind: The Sanitation Department lists the three carters authorized for your commercial waste zone and shows the maximum price each may charge.
suppliers.examples: The three carters authorized for your commercial waste zone
suppliers.note: Seen at the Sanitation Department: three carters are authorized in each of the 20 zones, and a calculator shows each carter's maximum monthly rate.

suppliers.what: Architect or engineer to file plans, licensed plumber and electrician, general contractor with cafe experience
suppliers.whereToFind: Ask who built the cafes you admire, check licenses with the Department of Buildings, and get three written bids that say whether equipment hookups are included.
suppliers.examples: Licensed general contractors with food-service projects; the city offers free plan examinations for small businesses
suppliers.note: Seen in a contractor's 2026 guide: counter-service cafe build-outs in former food spaces run $200-$300 per sq ft, permits 6-14 weeks, construction 8-24 weeks. Names are well-known examples from general knowledge of the New York market, not endorsements and not checked in this session unless a link is given; compare at least three quotes.

lessons.title: Labor above the norm
lessons.lesson: Labor should be near 35% of sales. Schedule people to the hours that sell.

lessons.title: Rent above the norm
lessons.lesson: Rent should be near 10% of sales. Negotiate, pick a cheaper block, or plan the sales that justify the address.

realLife.note: The game waits only for the two Health Department items (21 days). In real life the build-out sets the date: permit path 6-14 weeks, long-lead equipment 8-20 weeks, construction 8-24 weeks, inspections 1-3 weeks (contractor's 2026 estimates, steps overlap). The research notes budget three paid months of rent before opening for a former cafe and six for a heavy conversion.

risks.title: 12 weeks of rent with no sales
risks.why: From the lease to the first sale took 81 days (former cafe: light renovation, keeps the plumbing and ventilation). In real life budget 3 months of rent: $17,843.
risks.fix: Negotiate free rent for the build-out and apply for every permit the week you sign.

risks.title: Rent of $5,948 is above 10% of your sales
risks.why: In your season rent took 13% of sales. $10,740 over 4 months went to the landlord beyond the norm.
risks.fix: Ask for free months and a cap on increases, or plan the sales that pay for this address.

risks.title: 4 coffee shops share your passers-by
risks.why: 4 real ones within 150 m split the same 4,440 people a day. The nearest, 787 Coffee, is 90 m away.
risks.fix: Walk the block at 8am and at 2pm before you sign; count their lines and their prices.
